page: Google Cloud Platform c4d-highmem-2 is a general-purpose virtual machine configuration engineered with an elevated memory-to-vCPU allocation. Utilizing the x86_64 architecture, this instance is provisioned with 2 dedicated vCPUs and 15.0 GB of system memory, providing 7.5 GB of RAM per vCPU. The dedicated core allocation ensures consistent compute cycles without the thread contention or throttling typical of shared-core burstable instances.

Hardware resource provisions exclude local disk storage and discrete graphics accelerators, meaning all persistent storage workflows rely entirely on remote network-attached block volumes. Because local storage is absent and zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses are assigned by default, deployments require appropriate VPC routing and external block volume attachments for functional operation.

From an operational cost perspective, the instance is positioned for memory-heavy entry-tier services that do not demand extensive CPU parallelism. Allocating 15 GB across two dedicated cores provides efficient resource utilization for low-concurrency caching tiers, small relational databases, memory-resident microservices, and intermediate data transformation tasks where memory density takes precedence over raw compute capacity.
description: Google Cloud Platform c4d-highmem-2 is an x86_64 architecture virtual machine tailored for memory-centric operational workloads within the general-purpose category. The system provides 2 dedicated vCPUs accompanied by 15.0 GB of total RAM, delivering a 7.5 GB per core allocation ratio. This elevated memory configuration supports services requiring substantial runtime memory without mandating high core counts. The instance includes no integrated local storage, requiring persistent operational data to be maintained via network-attached block storage volumes, and does not incorporate GPU acceleration. By delivering dedicated CPU scheduling alongside an expansive memory footprint for a dual-core instance, c4d-highmem-2 functions as an efficient host for small relational databases, distributed cache layers such as Redis, lightweight in-memory data processing pipelines, and memory-intensive background microservices that operate under moderate processing concurrency.
